fields.title: Veha: Investor Suggests Entering a Large Market
fields.summary: An adjacent segment is three times larger than ours. Decide whether to go there.
fields.decisionPrompt: Will you enter taxi fleets, and what will you propose for the year?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Veha.
fields.brief/company: Vekha is a fictional fleet management system: routes, fuel, maintenance. 240 clients, average fleet of 30 cars, average bill of 24 thousand rubles per month.
fields.brief/context: An investor suggests entering taxi fleets: by his estimate, the market is three times larger than ours. The founder supports this. The annual plan is approved in a month.
fields.brief/objective: Decide whether to enter the new segment and under what conditions.
fields.brief/constraints: A team of 22 people. The annual budget allows for one major direction, not two.
fields.brief/task: Choose a solution and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A large market is not the same as an addressable market
fields.learnTakeaway/body: The decision to enter is based on three numbers: how much they are willing to pay, what it costs to serve them, and what channel gets you in. Market size is not one of them. And before looking for a new segment, it is worth checking your share in the current one: a share of a few percent means the ceiling is not the market, but your own execution.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
240 clients, 5.76 million ₽ per month. Growth of 4% per month, organic—half of new clients come from referrals.

Profit by group after deducting support:
construction and trading companies with fleets of 20–60 vehicles—168 clients, 71% of profit;
fleets under 20 vehicles—54 clients, operating near break-even, support costs are as high as for large ones;
fleets over 100 vehicles—18 clients, require custom work, total profit slightly above zero.

Annual churn is 6%—low: years of fuel consumption data make switching expensive.

Strength confirmed by numbers: connecting a vehicle takes 15 minutes compared to several hours for our two known competitors—thanks to integration with the two most popular tracker models.
fields.evidenceCards/1/title: What is known about taxi fleets
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Shift tracking and driver payouts—something we don't have at all. Estimate: 5 months of team capacity.

Integration with aggregators: technically possible, but according to our information, access is granted only to partners, and negotiations take at least six months.

Support: a taxi fleet contacts support on average 4 times more often than our current client—according to two out of five owners who have experience with other systems.

With a check of 3–8 thousand ₽ per fleet and this level of support, the margin is negative across the entire range quoted by owners.

Meanwhile, in our current segment, there is an untested opportunity: 43 deals lost over the year due to lack of integration with fuel card accounting systems. Estimate—6 weeks.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Investor: «Your market is small, you will hit a ceiling in two years».

The founder supports the expansion and has already announced it in an interview with an industry publication.

Commercial Director: «We have a queue of construction companies, but no one to sell to—we are short-handed».

Sales: we turned down 43 clients over the year due to fuel cards; all of them were from the profitable segment.

Prices haven't been raised in two years.

In our current segment, we estimate there are 6,400 companies of suitable size; we work with 240, meaning we occupy less than 4%.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Stay in your segment and break through its ceiling
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Show with calculations that entering taxi fleets is unprofitable given their willingness to pay, and invest the year in what already brings profit: fuel cards, pricing, and market share.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The calculation ends the argument without emotion: with a check of 3–8 thousand ₽ per fleet and four times more frequent support, the margin is negative across the entire range, and the segment leaders grew through partnerships with aggregators, where negotiations take at least six months.
The second number dismantles the ceiling argument: there are 6,400 suitable companies in the current segment, and we have 240—less than 4%. The ceiling is not close.
You release fuel cards in 6 weeks: 43 lost deals per year return to the pipeline, all from the profitable group.
You raise prices for new clients for the first time in two years, and move fleets under 20 vehicles to a tariff that covers support costs.
Over the year, revenue grows by +52%, while churn remains at 6%.
Compromise: the founder had already announced the entry in an interview, so you had to explain a public pivot; relations with the investor grew colder.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The market is three times larger, and the investor and founder are in favor. Build shift tracking in five months and start selling.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
For five months, the team is busy with shift tracking, and the current segment does not develop.
Initial sales are tough: fleets compare us with aggregator systems that are free for them, bargaining down to 3 thousand ₽.
Over six months, 26 fleets are connected; their support load is comparable to the entire rest of the customer base.
With this price and support load, every new fleet reduces profit.
At the same time, 43 deals in the profitable segment are lost again—fuel cards were never built.
Compromise: market size was confused with addressable share; entry was paid for with a year of work in the segment where we make money.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Replicate the product of segment leaders
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The two leaders have already found what fleets need. Replicate their offering—shift tracking, driver payouts—and enter with a lower price.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Functionally, you manage to replicate it, and the product looks just as good.
But the leaders didn't grow because of the product: aggregators integrated them into the fleet dashboard, and that is where clients come from. This channel is closed to us—negotiations take at least six months and only with partners.
Without this channel, sales are one-off and expensive, and a price lower than the leaders makes the economics even worse.
By the end of the year, there are 19 connected fleets and a negative margin for this direction.
Compromise: you copied the storefront, not the growth mechanism; meanwhile, using a low price to enter amplified the main problem.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Test the segment with a cheap bet
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Don't build shift tracking right away. Build a minimal version for a few fleets manually, sell to five to ten, and look at the numbers.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The bet is honest and costs one month instead of five. Five fleets agree, and some of the work is done manually.
The numbers confirm the fears: they are willing to pay 4–6 thousand ₽, contact support frequently, and two of them leave for an aggregator system within two months.
You get proof instead of an argument and close the topic with data—which is better than deciding in a meeting room.
But a month was spent on what was already clear from five conversations and margin math, and fuel cards were delayed.
Furthermore, with only five fleets, you cannot distinguish between 'the segment is bad' and 'we sold poorly,' so part of the team remains unconvinced.
Compromise: useful caution bought with time that would have been enough to win back 43 deals.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: An external factor is named but not carried through to its logical conclusion for the decision
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: A strength is claimed without proof and without what it limits
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: A competitor is analyzed by feature set rather than growth mechanism
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Clients are not segmented by profit and cost of service
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: The financial decision was made without the math of pricing, churn, and expansion
